finding.claim: iconUrl, supplied by the user via PUT /profile, is stored without any validation and later fetched by the nightly sync job, allowing SSRF to internal hosts, cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/), or arbitrary URLs. The response is read as a byte array, so it may be exposed if the icon is served back to the user.
finding.sink: HttpClient.send with HttpRequest built from URI.create(iconUrl) at Profile.java:23

trace.note: this.iconUrl = icon stored with no validation
sync() builds GET request with URI.create(iconUrl)
c.send(...) issues the request; response body read at line 24

finding.guards_checked: Checked the regex validation at line 12. It applies only to webhook and not to icon. There is no scheme, host allowlist, or private-IP/metadata blocking for iconUrl. The HttpClient is passed in and its redirect/proxy configuration is not visible, so no mitigation is assumed. The webhook URL (line 21) is guarded by a full-match regex (String.matches anchors the whole string) that restricts it to https://hooks.example.com/ plus 20 alphanumerics, so it is not reported.

verdict.reason: The `icon` parameter is stored unvalidated at Profile.java:16, since the regex at line 12 checks only `webhook`, and is then fetched via `URI.create(iconUrl)` at Profile.java:23-24. No scheme or host check exists anywhere in the file, and no other file references `iconUrl`. Nothing in the code shows that the fetched icon is served back to the user, so the data-exposure part of the claim is speculative. The SSRF itself stands.
